A tall wall of wooden slats holds hundreds of plaster casts of words and syllables, among them the hushing sound of the title, and a troupe of dancers and musicians arranges, carries, drops and breaks them in repeated actions through the day.

The score and the physical routines push toward exhaustion: words pile up, get shouted, sung and smashed, and the performers keep going anyway. Fragile plaster is made to take rough treatment, so language reads as both material and burden.

It is the first time the pavilion has been given over mainly to performance, and the work is staged on set days with the installation left in place between them.

shows.title: Domus Diasporica
shows.description:
Mladen Bundalo, who left Bosnia and Herzegovina and lives abroad, makes a pavilion about what a home is once you live far from it. Rooms of an old Venetian palazzo are furnished like a domestic interior with a table, chairs and a rug, and a wall covered in wavy black lines like a map of flowing water or a grain.

Film, photographs and drawings sit among the furniture: slow video of half-built family houses in the countryside, a grid of snapshots of people at work in gardens, framed blue drawings of knotted forms, small shelves holding objects, and open books of photographs. The houses built by migrants for a return that may never come are a central image.

The work asks how belonging changes with history, money and politics, and treats diaspora as a way of living in two places at once.

shows.title: Comigo ninguém pode
shows.description:
Rosana Paulino and Adriana Varejão share the Brazilian pavilion, curated by Diane Lima, in a show that mixes works from three decades with pieces made for Venice. The title borrows the name of a houseplant, the dieffenbachia, kept by the door in Brazilian homes as a charm against harm even though it is poisonous, and the show reads as a protective gesture aimed at a wounded history.

Paulino contributes clusters of white and terracotta forms that climb the walls, rows of drawings of women and hybrid figures, and a field of rusted rods carrying printed portraits. Varejão answers with her glazed-tile style faces in red, painted foliage and a ceiling work that turns the pavilion's concrete into part of the picture.

Both artists return to colonial violence, the Black and Indigenous body, and the stories written onto surfaces such as tile, fabric and skin. The pairing sets two long careers in conversation about memory, repair and the strength of the people who kept going.

shows.title: The Federation of Minor Practices
shows.artist: Gery Georgieva, Maria Nalbantova, Rayna Teneva, Veneta Androva
shows.description:
The Bulgarian pavilion is staged as the base of an imaginary research lab, the Federation of Minor Practices, in which care and attention replace sovereignty. A circular copper-clad table with touchscreen terminals sits in the first room and runs a computer game that gathers signals from four films.

The films are in a darkened screening room with cushions on the floor. Gery Georgieva works with digital myth and prophecy, Veneta Androva with disinformation and mushroom websites, Rayna Teneva with the Rose Valley where flower harvest and arms manufacture share a landscape, and Maria Nalbantova with long-term ecological care at the Dragoman Marsh.

The idea is to look back from an imagined future at the early twenty-first century as the moment such shared practices of care began to take shape.

venue.name: Bulgaria Pavilion
venue.address: Sala Tiziano at the Centro Culturale Don Orione Artigianelli, Fondamenta Zattere ai Gesuiti 919

shows.title: NZƎNDA - The Path Home
shows.artist: Beya Gille Gacha, Jail Time Records, Sylvie Njobati, Bienvenue Fotso, Zora Snake, Neals Niat
shows.description:
NZƎNDA is a Medumba word for the door or the way home, and the Cameroon pavilion is built as a path in twelve chapters rather than a conventional exhibition. Conceived by artist and curator Beya Gille Gacha, it moves through rooms of a Cannaregio foundation using textile, sculpture, sound, video and live performance.

Images from the show include figures wrapped in white cloth patterned with red and blue marks, banners hung before a flag, a landscape of mud bricks and small model buildings, and performers carrying framed images. Six contributors, including the collective Jail Time Records and artists Sylvie Njobati, Bienvenue Fotso, Zora Snake and Neals Niat, share the route.

The project treats Cameroon as a living body whose historical wounds are crossed on the way back home.

venue.name: Cameroon Pavilion
venue.address: Gervasuti Foundation, Calle Lunga Santa Caterina, Cannaregio 4998

shows.title: Abbas Akhavan: Entre chien et loup
shows.description:
Abbas Akhavan wraps the Canada Pavilion in glass and turns it into a giant Wardian case, the sealed plant carrier that once moved living specimens around the British Empire. Inside is a dark pool lit by purple grow lights and filled with Victoria water lilies, whose enormous floating pads and rare night blooms fill the room, with mist rising from the water.

The lily was a sensation of the Victorian age and was named for the queen, who was given a place in its story. Akhavan, whose work often digs into gardens, plants and the stories attached to them, uses it to look at Britain's empire, the Crystal Palace and Canada's place as a Commonwealth country. Around the pool he places a stack of logs and heavy stones, among them works from 2018, so the glasshouse reads as part garden, part artefact.

Curated by Kim Nguyen for the National Gallery of Canada, the title is a French phrase for dusk, the hour when a dog and a wolf can no longer be told apart.

shows.title: Inter-Reality
shows.description:
Norton Maza fills the Sala dell'Isolotto at the Arsenale with a white, faceted structure that looks like an aircraft or building run aground on a rock covered in moss. A boarding ladder leads up to it, a pilot's helmet sits on a frame, a falcon perches on a power-line tower, and inside, lit like lightboxes, are dioramas of burning landscapes, caves and flooded valleys.

The work plays with illusion and scale, so that what looks like a vast scene turns out to be a miniature and the sure ground of the visitor gives way. Maza uses these simulacra to talk about disinformation, migration, ecological crisis, war and the way competing versions of reality fragment what people can agree on.

The artist and curators place the project in a South American perspective, treating the pavilion as a space for sharing responsibility and for asking who controls the truth.

shows.title: Dream Stream
shows.artist: Game Science, Feng Ji, Yang Qi, Liu Chenglong, Wang Yixin+Wang Yu, Weng Jie, Lin Zhe, Zhou Haosong, Fei Si, Huang Chengxi, Yang Tingmu+Yang Hancheng+Xie Xianhui, Team of China Academy of Art and Zhejiang Lab, Xu Jiang, Wang Dongling, Yang Fudong, Lining Yao+Guanyun Wang+Danli Luo, Method Scenography Group (Mou Sen, Ma Yuanchi, Xin Ge, Mei Yuezi, Zhao Da), Wu Ziyang+Crude_Castin (Xu Jing, Zou Nan, Ye Qi, Yan Zhenghao), Nie Shichang, Jiang Suxuan+Yu Jiangfan, Hu Yueming+Lin Yuxin+Ji Huanhuan, Zhang Zhoujie
shows.description:
The Chinese pavilion is a dark, long Arsenale hall threaded with screens, light boxes and curved enclosures, built around the idea of the dream stream, a phrase taken from a Song dynasty scholar's notebook on art, science and the natural world. More than twenty participants from art, design, science and games share the space.

A wall of black-ink calligraphy by Wang Dongling faces a robot seated at a writing table, a bronze concentric disc sits beside a luminous grid of paper-like panels, and glowing dioramas of ruined landscapes sit next to painted panels, small screens and game footage. Outside, a mirrored garden and fields of bamboo and sunflowers carry the theme into the grounds. Game Science, the studio behind Black Myth: Wukong, appears in an art setting for the first time.

The show argues that technology can grow from cultural roots instead of breaking with them, and tries to stage tradition and innovation as one continuous current.

shows.title: Simba Moto! Seize the Fire! Saisis le feu !
shows.artist: Sammy Baloji, Arlette Bashizi, Patrick Bongoy, Damso, Gosette Lubondo, Nelson Makengo, Aimé Mpané, Léonard Pongo, Géraldine Tobé
shows.description:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo has its first national pavilion, a collective show by nine artists from Kinshasa, Goma and the diaspora, curated by Nadia Yala Kisukidi. It is set up as a forge: a blue-lit hall in a former refectory of the Scuola Grande di San Marco, hung with silvery sheeting, where fire stands for the power to shape and remake.

On view are tapestry-like and carpet works, ink drawings, large photographs, a transparent platform carrying figures made of matchstick stems by Aimé Mpané, and screens and sound. Sammy Baloji shows sculptures and collage prints that enlarge Congolese artworks, and photographers including Léonard Pongo and Arlette Bashizi work with night, landscape and portraiture.

The call of the title is to tell new stories of Congo that draw on older worldviews and Congolese imaginaries rather than lack, pain and death.

venue.name: Congo Pavilion
venue.address: Antico Refettorio - Scuola Grande di San Marco, Castello 6777

shows.title: Compelled by Fright and Beauty
shows.description:
Dubravka Lošić has worked for four decades in long-running cycles, and the Croatian pavilion reworks several of them for the rooms and courtyard of a Castello palazzo. Her series run from Libertas Bells, tied to her native Dubrovnik, to rosaries, sharks and rain over Paris, and move between painting, collage, metal and sculptural fabric.

The pictures show tied and knotted textile masses in deep blue, white and hot pink, quilted grey panels hung in a row down a gallery, rust-coloured cylinders in a courtyard, and round discs on brick walls. The pieces hold anxiety and beauty together without telling the viewer how to read them.

Curator Branko Franceschi frames the show as a look at how beauty, trauma and cultural position meet, and at how Central and Eastern European experience is read internationally.

shows.title: Hombres Libres / Free men
shows.description:
Roberto Diago fills the Cuba pavilion with a crowd of large sculpted heads built from salvaged wood, scrap metal, tin and old paint, their surfaces patched, stitched and scarred. They stand in a brick-vaulted gallery like a gathering of people, and visitors are allowed to touch them.

The work honours the Maroons who chose death over slavery and people who have risked everything for freedom, and it says that freedom is something kept up through daily practice. The patched faces also speak of life in present-day Cuba, where neighbours share clothes, shoes and food.

Two black polished heads on plinths, one of which also stands outside the entrance, give the installation a smooth, quiet counterpoint to the rough, colourful crowd.

venue.name: Cuba Pavilion
venue.address: Il Giardino Bianco – Art Space, Via Giuseppe Garibaldi, Castello 1814

shows.title: It rests to the bones
shows.description:
Marina Xenofontos builds the Cyprus pavilion around Passer, an animatronic female sparrow modelled on the mechanical automata of early modern Europe. The bird is stuffed, wired and set into motion, so a small creature becomes a stage for questions about stillness, labour and care.

Around it sit new sculptures in copper and other metals, including rolled and cylindrical forms placed on the floor of an old brick-walled hall, one of them with a motor and cable. One work reproduces a ceiling from a nightclub in the abandoned seaside district of Varosha.

The pavilion uses time and decay as its subject, letting objects that look inert slowly turn or move. It was chosen through an open call and curated by Kyle Dancewicz.

shows.title: The Silence of the Mole
shows.description:
For the first joint Czech and Slovak presentation in twenty years, the Giardini pavilion becomes a dark, quiet environment of architecture, sculpture and film. Selmeci Kocka Jusko line the building with black shelving, narrow corridors and slender metal and wood forms that stand like tools or instruments in a cellar, as though a hidden burrow had been built inside the white hall.

In the middle of it all stands a large screen showing a film by Jakub Jansa, made in answer to the duo's spaces. It follows an ageing actor who has spent decades playing a mole character, and moves through bright landscapes, crowds, rehearsal rooms and dreamlike scenes, so that the figure of the mole stands for a life lived out of public view.

The parts were made together and cannot be separated, which turns the pavilion into a single piece about hiddenness, performance and the long, slow work of digging.

shows.title: Things to Come
shows.description:
Maja Malou Lyse's pavilion is a glossy, deadpan science-fiction musical about fertility. A big video made with the collective DIS, set in a sperm bank in 2045, stars an adult-film performer as a lab scientist, and mixes clinical white-coat imagery with pop-video gloss and surreal humour. The film argues, half seriously, that a powerful enough image might change human reproduction.

Next door the pavilion becomes a kind of altar: rows of yellow cryogenic storage containers stand against pale lilac walls, and the show stages 'sperm races', inspired by online communities where young men turn worries about falling fertility into competitions.

The design studio Common Accounts shaped the cool blue and white interior. Curated by Chus Martinez, the pavilion takes the internet's strangest corners seriously as sources of myth, ritual and anxiety about the future.

shows.title: Tawna & Oscar
shows.description:
Ecuador's first national pavilion pairs the Tawna collective, an Amazonian group of Kichwa, Sápara and mestizo artists, with the artist Oscar Santillán. Tawna shows two films, Llaki and Kawashima, in which dreaming, sexuality and the making of clay vessels from forest earth become ways of holding territory and memory together.

Santillán's part of the show is Antimundo, a body of painting, sculpture and speculative installation where scientific and computational imagery meets bodies and raw materials. Twisting metal, stone and fabric objects sit on low plinths in rooms hung with dark green gauze, and a large swirling painting faces the films.

The two practices are kept distinct rather than blended, so the pavilion reads as two sets of ideas about knowledge and survival hung next to each other.

shows.title: Silence Pavilion: Between the Tangible and the Intangible
shows.description:
Armen Agop turns the Egyptian pavilion into a dim room for listening. Smooth dark stone forms, among them a tall blade-like monolith and low disc shapes resting on plinths or floating beneath a black oval, are lit by single beams of light, and a large blue and violet painting hangs on one wall.

Visitors are asked to enter quietly and to leave their phones in their pockets, and photography inside the room is discouraged. The aim is silence as a presence rather than an absence, something that can be shaped, held and shared.

The project links the sculptor's long engagement with stone and form to the Biennale's theme of minor keys, offering stillness and the barely visible in a fair that is otherwise loud.

shows.title: Cartographies of the Displaced
shows.description:
El Salvador's first pavilion at the Biennale is a set of tall, pale, tapering sculptures by José Oscar Molina, who left the country during the civil war in 1989 and now lives in New York state. The figures stand in a palazzo garden like a crowd, some capped with a small head or a bud-shaped tip.

The curator frames displacement as a lasting condition, not a single journey, and the forms suggest carrying, waiting and endurance more than arrival. The works do not document crossings; they give weight to what stays with people afterward.

shows.title: The Forest The Undergrowth
shows.artist: Fernando Nguema Madja, Modest Gené Roig, Rani Bruchstein, Barbara Cammarata, Florin Codre, Jianqi Du, Martin Emschermann, Alessia Forconi, Fulvio Merolli, Alfred Mirashi Milot, Mfochive Oumarou, Hannou Palosuo, Valeria Pérez Fuchs, Andrea Roggi, Sonia Ros, Carlotta Flora Saavedra González, Sandro Sanna, Giuseppe Saporito, Ingrid Seall, Michele Stanzione, Vassilis Vassiliades,  Liu Youju, William Marc Zanghi
shows.description:
Equatorial Guinea's first national pavilion fills Palazzo Donà dalle Rose with a group show of more than twenty artists, many of them Italian or based in Europe alongside Equatoguinean and other international names. It takes the forest of the country as its starting point and builds an imagined undergrowth, a layered world of plants, animals and spirits that visitors walk through.

The show ties into the Biennale's In Minor Keys theme by looking at small, hidden and overlooked forms of life, and it brings painting, sculpture, installation and film together under that idea.

shows.title: The House of Leaking Sky
shows.description:
Estonian painter Merike Estna turns the pavilion into an open studio and paints the space itself, so the show is made on site and keeps changing while it is open. A large drawing and painting spreads across the floor and walls in green, pink and black, with tiled patches, looping lines, sketched eyes and handwritten phrases, and finished canvases and boards sit among the working tools.

The curator presents painting as a live act in public rather than a finished object, and the visitor walks across the work as it develops.

shows.title: Shapes of Silence
shows.description:
Ethiopia's second national pavilion is a solo show of new paintings by Tegene Kunbi, an Addis Ababa-born artist based in Berlin. He builds thick, pigment-heavy surfaces from stripes and grids, and presses in fragments of woven cloth, rugs and found material so that patterns from Ethiopian textile and folk traditions surface through the paint.

The curator reads the works as a study of silence as a social and political condition, something shaped and carried rather than empty. Large yellow, red and blue panels hang in the vaulted rooms of Palazzo Bollani, with details of impasto and fabric close up.

shows.title: Aeolian Suite
shows.description:
Jenna Sutela turns Alvar Aalto's small Finnish Pavilion into a room full of wind. Tall, shaggy grey sculptures, made of fur and spikes and resembling the foam covers on microphones, hang and turn in a circle like the points of a wind rose. Fans, instruments and recordings drive the movement and the sound, which is composed from weather data and from winds recorded in Venice, Helsinki and elsewhere.

The work sets itself against noise cancelling and forecasting by treating wind as something that cannot be calculated or fully controlled. The five winds that shape the Venice lagoon, the Tramontana, two Boras, the Scirocco and the Garbin, become the characters of a sound piece that guides visitors through careful listening.

Curated by Stefanie Hessler for Frame Contemporary Art Finland, the pavilion marks seventy years of the Finnish building and ties the lagoon's changing air to wider questions about climate. It travels to the Oulu Art Museum in 2027.

shows.title: Comme Saturne
shows.description:
Yto Barrada reopens the French pavilion as a suite of rooms in which textiles, time and the planet Saturn set the pace. A dark-walled gallery holds embroidered and woven panels, flags and slogans, including a banner reading On a marché sur la tête, while a long band of woven marks reads like a score. A room of rippling cream curtains shelters a rock-like sculpture, framed drawings and a copper-coloured moon disc.

The pieces draw on weaving, dyeing, calendars and craft knowledge she has gathered across Morocco and elsewhere, and treat cloth as a way of recording days, labour and the sky. Saturn, the planet of slow cycles, supplies the title and the idea of a lengthy orbit.

The pavilion was curated by Myriam Ben Salah and produced with the Institut français, and it brings Barrada's long interest in archives, plants and craft into one carefully staged space.

shows.title: Modern Argonauts – Georgian Crossroads
shows.artist: Tatia Darchiashvili, Konstantin Mindadze, Guram Nikoladze, Nestan Mikeladze, Manuchar Okrostsvaridze, Guela Patiachvili, Mamuka Tsetskhladze, Merab Buliskiria, Karim Borjas, Jean-Dominique Ferrucci, Aliska Lahusen, Eve Ramboz, Annette Turrillo, Pedro Morales, Eizo Sakata, Mauro Marcenaro, Silvano Rubino
shows.description:
Modern Argonauts reworks the myth of Jason and the Golden Fleece, which Georgia claims as part of its own ancient story, as a picture of constant crossing and exchange instead of a return to origins. The curators bring Georgian artists together with artists from France, Poland, Venezuela, Japan, the United States and Italy, seventeen in all.

The rooms of Palazzo Querini mix a hanging world map on cloth, rows of ink and photographic panels, framed paintings, a wall of black-and-white glyph panels, a looping golden thread piece and a dark sculptural tree-like form. The idea is that Georgia is a crossroads where cultures meet and change one another.

venue.name: Georgia Pavilion
venue.address: Palazzo Querini - Calle Lunga San Barnaba, Dorsoduro 2691

shows.title: Ruin
shows.description:
Ruin fills the German Pavilion with the missing buildings of East German history: the vanished GDR pavilion at the Biennale, the demolished Palace of the Republic in Berlin, and the Sunflower House in Rostock, burned in the racist riots of 1992. Sung Tieu covers the neoclassical facade in a trompe-l'oeil mosaic of a decaying prefab block in Berlin where she grew up, a home for Vietnamese contract workers that later housed migrant families, and her sparse white rooms hold quiet, fragile floor and wall pieces.

Henrike Naumann's part, a mint-green installation called The Home Front, is a room of furniture, a frieze of chairs, a wall of household objects, a long wooden mural of figures and hanging costumed figures on ropes. It draws on the East German 1990s of baseball bats and rising far-right violence, treating taste and interior design as political evidence. Naumann died in February 2026, shortly before the Biennale opened.

Curated by Kathleen Reinhardt, the show treats the gaps left by erased buildings as zones where time broke, and imagines art as a form of resistance to that break.

shows.title: La Merde
shows.description:
Aline Bouvy's pavilion is built around a curved, mirrored enclosure and a film shown in an immersive, spatialised screening room. Standing in front of the mirror is a life-size white sculpture of E.T., its body morphed with the artist's own figure, caught facing its reflection.

The film La Merde works as a cinematic manifesto on shame as something society builds, and on the lines drawn around which bodies are accepted, policed or pushed out. It treats abjection and waste as forces that unsettle neat identities, with particular attention to how female bodies have been linked with excess and impurity.

Mirrors, sound and the dark viewing room make the visitor part of the setup, so the question of who looks at whom, and who is judged, stays open inside the old brick hall.

shows.title: Predicting History: Testing Translation
shows.description:
Lubaina Himid fills the British Pavilion with large, bright, multi-panelled paintings in which groups of working people stand around tables, benches and ladders, deep in discussion. They are architects, tailors, chefs and gardeners, and they seem to be arguing over whether to stay or go. Around these big scenes hang smaller framed paintings, a painted fly, a portrait in a wooden frame, and rows of painted oars and paddles along the walls.

Himid, a Turner Prize winner born in Zanzibar and based in the north of England, uses the show to ask what it means to make a home somewhere new and how the pull of belonging shows up in daily life. The grand neoclassical rooms look welcoming on first look, but sound, text and the figures' body language hint at unease and uncertainty.

She stages her paintings like scenes from a play, giving the characters lines and moods and leaving the viewer to complete the story, so that anyone walking in becomes part of the performance. The commission is led by Ese Onojeruo for the British Council.

shows.title: Escape Room
shows.description:
Andreas Angelidakis turns the Greek Pavilion into a strobe-lit, red-and-violet maze that works as both a game and a history lesson. Toppled stone columns and statues, wrapped in chains, spill down the front steps and hang inside; a glowing neon sign reading ESCAPE hangs over the entrance; vitrines and rails of garments, sports shirts, newspapers and little white figures act as clues scattered through the rooms.

The artist, an architect as well as an artist, borrows the idea of a Japanese-style escape room to reinterpret Plato's cave. Visitors piece together fragments of twentieth-century Greek and European politics to see how nations are built out of myths and then sold back as truth.

The pavilion's own past as a building becomes evidence, and the show treats nationalism, identity and history as staged, shifting stories rather than fixed facts.

shows.title: The Poetics of Correspondence
shows.artist: Edward Bowen, Arthur Daniel, Josine Dupont, Alexandra Kordas, Lilo Nido and Chris Mast, Jeverson Ramirez, The Holzwege Group, Russell Watson
shows.description:
Grenada's pavilion is a group exhibition curated by Daniel Radini Tedeschi in which eight artists or teams, from Grenada, the Caribbean and elsewhere, answer one another's work across painting, sculpture, photography, film and music. The title treats exchange between island and diaspora as a kind of letter-writing, with each piece a reply to another.

The press kit shows a compact gallery with works on the walls and small sculptures on plinths, alongside the steel-band culture of the islands and a digital image of a figure with a cloud of sand dispersing from the head.

shows.title: Las Invisibles
shows.artist: ARKEO, Luana Bottallo, Jorge Chavarría, Manuel Navichoc, Ana Lorena Núñez, SOY artistic group, Elsie Wunderlich
shows.description:
Las Invisibles gathers seven Guatemalan and Guatemala-linked artists around the people and things that hold daily life together without being noticed: women, hearth, corn, clay and stone. The works use fingerprints, glyph-like signs, portraits and sculpture to give those quiet roles a visible form.

On view are a large print built from a single fingerprint, a lightbox with a row of Maya-style glyphs, a framed portrait, and a round painted work with red threads running down the wall. The pavilion shares a building with Grenada's and is organised by two curators, Stefania Pieralice and Elsie Wunderlich, who also shows work.

shows.title: Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière
shows.artist: Francesco Tullio Altan, Paola Arrigoni, Bella Bah, Nino Barone, Stefania Basso, Emiliano Bazzanella, Giuliana Bellini, Milena Bellomo, Bluer (Lorenzo Viscidi), Alda Bòscaro, Alessandro Cadamuro, Carmine Calvanese, Carmela Candido, Giancarlo Caneva, Tommaso Cascella, Giancarlo Cazzaniga, Bruno Ceccobelli, Giorgio Celiberti, Giorgio Celiberti Jr., Maurizio Cervellati, Marco Ciani, Massimo Clemente, Bachir DiaIlo, Bruno Donzelli, Mauro Filigheddu, Mirko Filipuzzi, Pasquale Fraccalvieri, Ferruccio Franz, Carla Galli Morandi, Omar Galliani, Andrea Marco Ghia, King Emmanuel, Gianni Maglio, Paolo Marazzi, Rossella Marchesin, Marvin, Enzo Migneco (Togo), Zdravko Milić, Giampaolo Muliari, Lucia Paese, Bruno Paladin, Giorgio Pastres, Ottavio Pinarello, Giuseppina Pioli, Manuela Pittana, Adriano Piu, Stefano Pizzi, Claudia Raza, Rosaspina, Andrea Rossi Andrea, Marco Nereo Rotelli, Gernot Schmerlaib (BIX), Cesare e Noah Serafino, Alessio Serpetti, Leo Strozzieri, Sékou Oumar Thiam, Lucia Tomasi, Angelo Toppazzini, Maurizio Valdemarin, Andrea Vizzini, Luciana Zabarella, Marina Zambon, Tono Zancanaro, Leonardo Zanin
shows.description:
Guinea's first national pavilion is on the island of San Servolo, a former monastery and hospital, and brings together more than sixty mostly Italian artists around the idea of sound and matter. The title plays on the Biennale's In Minor Keys theme: works are meant to echo, vibrate or resonate through the materials they are made of.

The pictures released for the show are paintings and mixed-media works, among them a cubist-style acrylic of two figures by King Emmanuel, a collage with iron and plastic by Pasquale Fraccalvieri, a dark metal-and-canvas piece by Maurizio Cervellati and a swirl of green, red and yellow ink by Maurizio Valdemarin.

shows.title: Yelena's Garden 2025-2026
shows.description:
Haiti's pavilion is a garden-themed solo show by Enock Placide, titled Yelena's Garden 2025-2026, set in the frescoed rooms of Palazzo Albrizzi-Capello. His paintings are dense, glowing fields of flowers and sunsets, and he adds round painted panels and a sphere that read like small planets, so the garden spreads from the picture into a cosmos.

The project continues a long-running series, with work made over the last year. Close views of the blooms show the thick, saturated brushwork that carries the mood of the show.

shows.title: The Ear is the Eye of the Soul
shows.artist: Alexander Kluge, Benedictine Nuns of the Abbey of St. Hildegard Eibingen, Bhanu Kapil, Brian Eno, Carminho, Caterina Barbieri, Devonté Hynes, FKA Twigs, Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst, Ilda David’, Jim Jarmusch, Kali Malone, Kazu Makino, Laraaji, Meredith Monk, Moor Mother, Otobong Nkanga, Patti Smith, Precious Okoyomon, Raúl Zurita, Soundwalk Collective, Suzanne Ciani, Tatiana Bilbao Estudio, MAIO Architects & Dogma, Terry Riley
shows.description:
The Holy See's pavilion is built around sound rather than objects, taking its cue from the medieval nun and composer Hildegard of Bingen. Musicians, writers and filmmakers including Patti Smith, Brian Eno, FKA Twigs, Meredith Monk and Jim Jarmusch each contribute listening works that visitors hear while moving through a walled garden of vines, olive trees and pergolas.

A second site in Castello holds a set of small rooms built by architects with scaffolding, lamp-lit tables and shelves of screens, glowing yellow, where pieces can be listened to and read. Curated by Hans Ulrich Obrist and Ben Vickers with Soundwalk Collective, the show asks visitors to treat hearing as a form of spiritual attention.

venue.name: Holy See Pavilion
venue.address: Giardino Mistico dei Carmelitani Scalzi, Cannaregio 54

shows.title: pneuma cosmic
shows.description:
Endre Koronczi presents a fictional research project on air, in which his long interest in wind and breath is treated as if it were a scientific programme. The pavilion is dominated by a heap of dark ventilation units taken from the listed Hungarian Academy of Sciences building, stacked and angled like a cliff of loudspeakers, alongside screens, texts and drawings, and a fumarole that echoes the huffing of the Earth's crust.

The artist walked for a year in search of the most important sigh, and the pavilion's own breath is rendered as a minimalist kinetic installation at the edge of what can be perceived. A site-specific soundscape by composer Máté Balogh frames the whole.

Curated by Luca Cserhalmi, the project sets scientific method against metaphor, offering a loosely drawn hypothesis about an air that connects human sighs and planetary currents rather than a proof.

shows.title: Pocket Universe
shows.description:
Icelandic artist, poet and composer Ásta Fanney Sigurðardóttir fills a former dockyard hall with a deep blue world made of sound, film, sculpture and performance. A screening room shows a snow-covered peak and a ghostly figure under the lights, a lone chair on a plinth sits in a dark room, and a wall carries wool tufts strung on barbed wire like notes on a stave.

The title asks what you would keep in a pocket the size of a universe. A pale shell-like sculpture of felted material and a table of small yellow forms suggest answers, and live performances and sound pieces are scheduled across the run, so the space changes while it is open.

shows.title: Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home
shows.artist: Alwar Balasubramaniam, Sumakshi Singh, Ranjani Shettar, Asim Waqif, Skarma Sonam Tashi
shows.description:
Five Indian artists each build a different kind of home inside the Arsenale. Alwar Balasubramaniam, known as Bala, sets a huge wall of cracked clay that reads as dried earth, a record of land under strain. Sumakshi Singh recreates her family's demolished house in Delhi at full scale in embroidered thread, so doors, windows and brickwork appear as a ghostly web of lines.

Ranjani Shettar hangs an airy garden of oversized white and golden flowers overhead, drawing on the place of plants in Indian life. Skarma Sonam Tashi stacks papier-mache houses into a Ladakhi hillside village, a reminder of traditional building under pressure from development. Asim Waqif's tangle of salvaged bamboo suggests scaffolding and the rapid, restless growth of cities.

Curated by Amin Jaffer, the show treats home as something carried in memory and gesture rather than a fixed address, and marks India's return to the Biennale after several years away.

shows.title: Printing the Unprinted
shows.artist: Agus Suwage, Syahrizal Pahlevi, R.E. Hartanto, Nurdian Ichsan, Theresia Agustina Sitompul (Terre), Mariam Sofrina, Rusyan Yasin
shows.description:
Indonesia's pavilion, its return after six years, is set in a printmaking school and built around an invented 15th-century manuscript about a great voyage. Seven artists spent a month in residence at the school and made new prints, drawings and objects there that read as pages and plates from that imagined archive.

A large open book sits on a patterned stand, framed lithographs and drawings line dark corridors, and rows of small white plaster heads are fixed to the brick of the courtyard wall. Agus Suwage contributes a mixed-media work on old paper showing a crocodile with a figure in its jaws, annotated like a natural-history page. The show asks what history looks like if the printed record was never made.

shows.title: Dreamshook
shows.description:
Isabel Nolan fills a bright Arsenale hall with hand-tufted tapestries, steel sculptures, furniture and drawings that move between cosmology, myth and daily life. Two large tapestries, one an arched sunrise over a wavy sea with a winged central figure and another a nocturnal arched scene of a house and gardens, face a patterned floor sculpture and a white steel frame shaped like a court or table.

Slender painted steel pieces stand like curtains, doorways and church windows, framing the room and the visitor, while a low wooden table and framed sheets of pale drawings sit nearby. Together they create a place that feels half ritual space and half domestic interior, with colour and scale shifting between wonder and unease.

Nolan's work asks how people find their place in a vast universe and an unstable world, and the pavilion offers both humour and tenderness in answer.

shows.title: Rose of Nothingness
shows.description:
Belu-Simion Fainaru presents a large water installation in a brick hall of the Arsenale: a shallow, dark basin set into the floor, with water falling drop by drop from a grid of points overhead so that ripples spread across a still black surface. The piece was first made in 2015 and has been shown in Berlin and at Art Basel; here it is reworked at pavilion scale among the old stone pillars.

The artist describes it as a quiet void, open to many readings, and it ties to his long use of Jewish ritual, history and loss as material. Ripples and reflections turn the room into a place for slow looking.

The pavilion has been the focus of boycott calls and protests during the Biennale, and the Giardini building stayed closed, with the work moved to the Arsenale.

shows.title: Con te con tutto
shows.description:
Chiara Camoni fills the Italian Pavilion with figures she and collaborators shape by hand from clay and earth, then dress or crown with plants, flowers, twigs, plastic and found debris. In the dim first Tesa, twenty-four life-sized standing sculptures stand like silent guardians, some capped with fresh cut flowers, some bristling with leaves or branches, so that living and inert matter sit side by side.

The second Tesa is bright and low: cabinets, tables, benches and floor pieces hold the smaller works of her ongoing Dialogues series, with places to sit and talk, and the largest of these resting areas opens toward the garden outside. Camoni's practice is communal, built from friendships, family and neighbours, and the show treats the studio as a chorus rather than a solo voice.

It matters because it carries a long, quiet, craft-based practice onto the national stage, favouring warmth, slowness and shared making over spectacle.

shows.title: Grass Babies, Moon Babies
shows.description:
Ei Arakawa-Nash fills the Japan Pavilion with some 200 baby dolls that climb scaffolds, hang from ropes, cling to rocks and sit among screens playing film excerpts. The dolls stand in for a new generation, and the show grows out of the artist becoming a parent of twins and treating care as a form of art making.

Visitors collect a doll at the entrance, move through the garden and the rooms, and at the end change a diaper to receive a poem written from the doll's birthday. A soundtrack of the twins' voices runs through the building, and the films raise questions about what counts as Japanese identity.

The project marks the pavilion's 70th anniversary and answers the architecture of Yoshizaka Takamasa, whose idea of unity built from separate parts becomes a model for shared responsibility toward the children who will inherit the present.

shows.title: Qoñyr: The Archive of Silence
shows.artist: Ardak Mukanova, Akmaral Mergen, ADYR-ASPAN (Gulmaral Tattibayeva, Natalia Ligay), Anar Aubakir, Asel Kadyrkhanova, Smail Bayaliyev, Nurbol Nurakhmet, Mansur Smagambetov, Oralbek Kaboke
shows.description:
Kazakhstan's third Biennale pavilion, chosen for the first time through an open call, takes its name from a traditional kyui, a short piece for the dombra, and builds a space about quiet, memory and soft sound. Visitors pass from a courtyard with tall, bark-textured sculptures of stitched and moulded material into dark rooms of film, painting, textile and sound.

A screen shows a musician playing, another room has large black, white and blue figure paintings around a low table, and a red hanging cloth marks the transition. Triptych projections of landscape and faces close the route. The curator links the project to In Minor Keys by treating silence as an archive of lived experience. An open letter has protested the removal of one planned work (Asel Kadyrkhanova's Machine), so the show differs from the approved line-up.

shows.title: Liberation Space: Fortress/Nest
shows.description:
The Korean pavilion is treated as a living monument to the years between liberation in 1945 and the founding of a state in 1948, a period when the country's shape was still open. Goen Choi, working with Thirdhand, runs slim copper rods across the white interior and out onto the grounds, so lines of force seem to cut through walls, ceiling and hedge. Hyeree Ro, with collaborators, fills the rest with a curving wall of hexagonal cells, low wooden seating, and delicate stands holding ceramics, scissors, cords and small objects.

Choi's work, called Meridian, thinks of the pavilion as a fortress made of shifting forces, while Ro's Bearing offers a softer nest of embrace. A group of bearers carries out a daily procession around the building for the whole run, adding a performed layer to the objects.

The project asks what a monument could be if it were not fixed in stone but kept alive through care, repetition and shared labour.

shows.title: Hard Teeth
shows.description:
Kosovo's pavilion is a single immersive painting by Brilant Milazimi, nearly seventeen metres long, set up in the nave of the church of Santa Maria del Pianto. Red hills and a blue sky run across a series of free-standing panels, with groups of pale human figures standing and waiting in the landscape.

The curator reads the work as a monument to waiting, a political and psychological state shaped by uncertainty, and the title Hard Teeth points to endurance. Visitors walk around the panels and see the scene from both sides.

venue.name: Kosovo Pavilion
venue.address: Chiesa di Santa Maria del Pianto, Fondamente Nove, Castello 6601/B

shows.title: Belek
shows.description:
Alexey Morosov, a sculptor born in Bishkek and based in Lucca, fills a deconsecrated Cannaregio church with the idea of belek, the Kyrgyz word for a gift. The gift in question is water: how a small mountain nation guards the most precious resource of the century while keeping hold of its memory and its land.

Two images carry the story. One is kok-boru, the horseback sport in which riders and horses read as a single centaur-like body. The other is the oral epic of Manas, chanted in a trance-like flow. Projections combine footage of Kyrgyz dams and kok-boru training with Morosov's marble-like figures, which sit among the church's altars and outside in the streets.

The show is Kyrgyzstan's second dedicated Venice presentation and reflects Morosov's long habit of setting classical sculptural language against industrial and technological material.

venue.name: Kyrgyz Republic Pavilion
venue.address: Ex Chiesa di Santa Caterina, Convitto Foscarini, Cannaregio 4941

shows.title: Untamed Assembly: Backstage of Utopia
shows.description:
The Latvian pavilion is built as a backstage. Forests of chrome clothing rails, hangers bent into wires and small metal birds fill the room, with garments, printed bags and a few folding chairs hung and set among them, and the whole thing sits behind long curtains in the colours of a stage wing.

The artist duo MAREUNROL'S made the installation in dialogue with the archive of Untamed Fashion Assemblies, the experimental fashion events that designer Bruno Birmanis staged in Riga in the 1990s, when the country was moving out of Soviet rule. Newly digitised footage from those shows plays on screens set into the racks, alongside books and photographs from the period.

The project looks at how groups imagine a different future while still behind the scenes, with scarcity, travel and open borders as the forces that made the events possible. The clothing rail becomes both a storage device and the architecture for those stories.

shows.title: Don't Get Me Wrong
shows.description:
Nabil Nahas hangs 26 acrylic-on-canvas panels in one unbroken frieze, some 45 metres long, around a dark blue room. The panels move between a lone cedar against snow and blue sky, gold-leafed branches, white spirals, fields of stars, and surfaces thick with red and white paint.

His pictures mix figuration with geometry and fractal patterns, and draw on Roman, Byzantine, Christian and Islamic imagery to suggest a layered, shared inheritance rather than a single identity. The tree is a nod to Lebanon, but it sits among cosmic forms that shrink human beings to a speck inside a vast order.

The room is lit and arranged to slow visitors down, so the paintings act as a field of energy to stand inside rather than a sequence to be read.

shows.title: animism sings anarchy
shows.description:
Eglė Budvytytė's new work for Lithuania is a three-channel film installation shot on 16 mm and shown as 4K projection. It turns the archaeology of Marija Gimbutas, who studied Neolithic goddess-centred societies, into song, gesture and trance-like movement rather than into lecture or reconstruction.

Filming took place inside the Museo delle Civiltà in Rome and along the Apulian coast near Grotta Scaloria, where Gimbutas dug in the late 1970s at a Neolithic water cult site. Performers lie in rock-cut pools, press photocopied deities to their chests and move between museum rooms and sea caves, as if rehearsing an animist prayer.

Facsimiles of ancient figurines, 3-D printed and photocopied, act as devotional centres for the choreography. In the Venice room the films are joined by a pale yellow boomerang-like floor sculpture, so visitors are invited to join the gathering as well as watch it.

venue.name: Lithuania Pavilion
venue.address: Fucina del Futuro, Calle San Lorenzo, Castello 5063/B

shows.title: No Need To Sparkle; Experiments in Love and Revolution
shows.artist: Adrian MM Abela, Charlie Cauchi, Raphael Vella
shows.description:
Malta's pavilion is built around three new film-based works, one from each artist, set in a dark Arsenale space where screens, sculpture and drawings share the floor. The films move between fiction and fact: a Roman-style bust and a costumed statue stand beside footage of café scenes, seaside landscapes and a figure in white on a beach.

The organising idea is to doubt well, meaning to question political certainty without giving up on action. The artists work from archives, cinema, pop culture and religious and historic texts, and the title borrows a line of thinking from Virginia Woolf. Small objects, such as a coin balanced on a table and a compressed cube of salvaged material, sit among the screens.

The show is notable as Malta's fifth outing at the main art exhibition, and Charlie Cauchi is the first woman to represent the country there.

shows.title: Actos invisibles para sostener el universo
shows.description:
RojoNegro, the duo of María Sosa and Noé Martínez, turns Mexico's Arsenale space into a low, hushed ritual ground. Curving banks of salt and clay wind across the floor, holding ceramic vessels, some shaped like animals and masked heads, that look like offerings left in a field.

Projected figures hover above the earthworks, and a video of a body moving slowly on the ground sets a breathing rhythm for the room. Tobacco, salt and clay are used for their old roles in protection, offering and altered states of mind.

The work draws on Indigenous, Afro-Mexican and rural ideas of how the world is held together by small, unseen acts, and offers visitors a place for contemplation away from the noise of the rest of the Biennale.

shows.title: On the Thousand and Second Night
shows.description:
Moldova's first official Biennale pavilion belongs to Pavel Brăila, who fills a small chapel with handwoven carpets that hang in mid-air, held aloft by drones. The idea grows out of his Magic Carpet of 2018, in which a single rug was lifted the same way.

The carpets come from different parts of Moldova, and some were bought elsewhere. The biggest belongs to the artist's aunt. Each one carries family memory and domestic ritual, which Brăila sets against the machines that now signal war and surveillance. In his telling the drones do not watch or threaten, they carry and protect.

Curated by Adelina Luft, the project sits inside the church complex of Santi Geremia e Lucia, and the chapel's altar and vault become part of the work. A panel discussion is planned there on 15 November.

venue.name: Moldova Pavilion
venue.address: Spazio Santa Veneranda, Chiesa dei Santi Geremia e Lucia, Cannaregio 272

shows.title: Entanglements: Connectivities Across Borders
shows.artist: Gerelkhuu Ganbold, Dorjderem Davaa, Nomin Bold, Tuguldur Yondonjamts
shows.description:
Four Mongolian artists work together on a pavilion about links across borders, starting from the thirteenth-century exchanges between the Mongols and Venice. The show sets those old networks of trade and diplomacy against present-day divisions.

Gerelkhuu Ganbold paints dense, layered scenes in the Mongol zurag manner. Nomin Bold makes textile works that hint at porous borders and the cycle of life and death. Dorjderem Davaa works in felt, and Tuguldur Yondonjamts adds multimedia and moving-image pieces.

It sits in the Squero Castello boatyard in Castello and is curated by Uranchimeg Tsultem and Thomas Eller.

shows.title: Out of the Blue, I’m Swept Away
shows.description:
Siniša Radulović's installation for Montenegro asks what a constant flood of images does to the way people see themselves and the world. The room is split in two: a low, moulded, basement-like zone and an upper, airy, fluid zone filled with moving and projected images.

The cherry blossom is one of the main motifs, standing for the fragility of existence. It appears as a branch of light thrown on the floor, alongside framed dark photographs, a lone sculpted figure under a spotlight and glowing, blurred light images.

The work is large and heavy (over nine tonnes, by one report) and sits in the new ArteNova space in Castello, moving the pavilion to a different venue from earlier years. It asks visitors to treat the space between private memory and public image as something they walk through.

venue.name: Montenegro Pavilion
venue.address: Spazio Artenova, Campo San Lorenzo, Castello 5063

shows.title: Asǝṭṭa
shows.description:
Morocco's first national pavilion fills a section of the Arsenale with large woven and knotted hangings by Amina Agueznay, made together with weavers and craftspeople from across the country. Bands of wool and cotton in cream, ochre, brick red and slate blue carry triangle patterns, while rope-like loops of red cord form dense, rounded motifs that hang like curtains.

The title refers to thresholds, and the visitor walks between cloth walls and a tall carved wooden post as if passing through a series of doorways. The work treats craft knowledge as something handed on from person to person, with hundreds of makers' hands visible in the surfaces.

It is a quiet, tactile piece that suits the Biennale's theme of minor keys, and it marks Morocco's arrival as a country with its own pavilion.

shows.title: AIM Inundated: Imagining Life After Land
shows.artist: Kauw Tsitsi, CPS (Khaled Ramadan, Alfredo Cramerotti), Patricia Jacomella Bonola, Tedo Rekhviashvili, Sylvia Grace Borda, Ron Laboray, Dorian Batycka, Khaled Hafez, Iv Toshain, Stefano Cagol
shows.description:
Nauru's first national pavilion treats disappearance as a cultural and political question rather than a spectacle of disaster. Ten artists and a curatorial collective approach the island nation, whose land has been stripped by phosphate mining and now faces rising seas, as an early example of loss, adaptation and resilience.

The structure follows archipelagic thinking: many voices, many islands, connected by water. Stefano Cagol's video We Are All Nauru stages symbolic acts of violence and exorcism in Greenland, Kyrgyzstan and Texas, and his Ice Monolith was shown again on the Venetian waterfront during the opening days. Ron Laboray contributes drawings and images.

Khaled Ramadan curates with associate curators Camilla Boemio and Stefano Cagol. A two-volume catalogue is launched on 19 November at the Querini Stampalia Foundation.

shows.title: The Fortress
shows.description:
Dries Verhoeven closes the Dutch pavilion from the outside, fitting the Rietveld building with steel shutters so its sunlit glass walls become a blank, defensive shell. Inside, the white rooms are emptied and darkened, and performers take over the space in rotation.

The performers stand on small white stools, press themselves into corners, cry out and hide under cloth, while on the floor sit odd small objects such as a cigarette-box-sized case and a post set in a tray. The work is about the reflex to protect oneself when the world feels unsafe, and it questions what a national pavilion means.

It is the first time live performance has been the whole programme in the Dutch pavilion, and the first time the building itself is part of the piece. The pavilion is closed on Tuesdays and on open Mondays, though it stays visible from outside as a sculpture.

shows.title: Taharaki Skyside
shows.description:
Fiona Pardington's Taharaki Skyside is a set of seventeen very large photographs of taxidermied birds (manu) held in museum collections in Aotearoa New Zealand and Australia. Many are rare, endangered or extinct, among them the laughing owl and the kakapo.

Each bird is lit and framed like a formal portrait, set against deep black and fitted with a coloured frame. The pictures draw on the memento mori tradition, but they also carry the Maori view of birds as ancestors and go-betweens, so that specimens kept behind glass become presences with faces.

The pavilion is presented by Creative New Zealand and Christchurch Art Gallery, in a former children's institute in Castello, and the work will go on to Christchurch in 2027.

venue.name: New Zealand Pavilion
venue.address: Istituto Provinciale per I’Infanzia Santa Maria della Pietà, Castello 3698

shows.title: How Many Angels Can Dance on the Head of a Pin?
shows.artist: Benjamin Orlow, Klara Kristalova, Tori Wrånes
shows.description:
The Nordic Pavilion, a low modernist hall built around living trees, becomes a stage for three artists whose figures seem caught mid-transformation. Klara Kristalova populates a giant fallen log with small ceramic and bronze creatures: a fox, a mouse in round ears, a crow beside a sleeping girl's head, an apple, winged fairies. They sit between fairy tale and nightmare, and a bronze owl watches from the pavilion's outer wall.

Benjamin Orlow's Ritual City is built in place from raw clay, a figure on scaffolding that slowly crumbles into a heap of bricks and dust over the run. Tori Wrånes contributes soft, stuffed, clothed bodies that bend, climb and hang from the architecture, including a pale figure arching over the entrance steps, together with sound and performance.

Curated by Anna Mustonen and shared by Finland, Norway and Sweden, the pavilion uses the cramped, tree-filled building as a pressure chamber where bodies, materials and memory reshape one another.

shows.title: Pietà in the Emergency Blankets
shows.description:
Velimir Zernovski wraps a sculpted Pieta in gold emergency blankets, the thin foil sheets first developed for space missions and now handed to people fleeing wars and disasters. The covering turns an image of Christian grief into a figure of present-day suffering.

The work, shown in a former chapel in Castello, also includes drawing and moving image. Gold foil wrinkles and catches light, so the figure reads as both precious and temporary, a shelter that is also a shroud.

The pavilion is organised by the Museum of Contemporary Art, Skopje, with curators Tihomir Topuzovski and Amanda Boetzkes.

venue.name: North Macedonia Pavilion
venue.address: Ex Cappella IPAB Buon Pastore, Castello 77

shows.title: Zīnah (Adornment)
shows.description:
Haitham Al Busafi's pavilion is a single immersive environment in a darkened Arsenale hall. Hundreds of silver-toned ornaments hang from above like a dense canopy, and below them a circle of pale sand lies on the floor, lit so that footprints and shadows show clearly.

The hanging pieces are based on the metal adornments traditionally placed on Omani horses. Visitors are asked to walk slowly, and their movement activates sound in the space. Drawings made by students and emerging artists in a workshop in Muscat are inscribed on some of the metal elements, so the piece carries many hands, not just the artist's.

It turns a regional craft of decoration into a room about listening, presence and mutual recognition.

shows.title: Punj•ab – A Sublime Terrain
shows.description:
Faiza Butt's pavilion looks at Punjab, the region split between Pakistan and India in 1947, as a layered landscape shaped by rivers, crops, empires and memory. Large textiles across nine chapters of the region's history anchor the show, together with tapestries, paintings and video.

The works were made with women artisans, and the pavilion treats that collaboration as shared authorship. Geotagged Pakistani minerals such as black quartz stand in where gemstones might be expected.

This is Pakistan's second Biennale pavilion, after its first in 2019. Beatriz Cifuentes Feliciano is curator.

venue.name: Pakistan Pavilion
venue.address: Ex Farmacia Solveni, Fondamenta Priuli, Dorsoduro 993-994

shows.title: Tropical Hyperstition
shows.artist: Antonio José Guzmán and Iva Jankovic – Messengers of the Sun
shows.description:
Messengers of the Sun, the duo of Antonio José Guzmán and Iva Jankovic, build a monumental hammock-like net in the Arsenale, lit in deep blue. It is meant as a structure of refuge, memory and survival, and it revisits the history of the Panama Canal through migration and the displacement of communities.

The pair work in indigo-dyed textile, sound and performance, drawing on the Black Atlantic and the African diaspora. A performance opened the pavilion in May.

It is Panama's second national pavilion, after its debut in 2024, and is curated by Ana Elizabeth González and Mónica E. Kupfer.

venue.name: Panama Pavilion
venue.address: Tesa 42 Arsenale, Fondamenta Case Nuove, Castello 2738/c

shows.title: Sara Flores. From Other Worlds
shows.description:
Sara Flores, a Shipibo-Konibo painter in her seventies, is the first Indigenous artist to represent Peru in Venice. Her pavilion in the Arsenale is a hall of large cotton canvases covered in kené, the dense geometric line patterns that Shipibo-Konibo women have long put on cloth, pottery and skin.

Each painting is a field of interlocking labyrinths, stepped crosses and mirrored motifs in black, rust, ochre and pink, drawn freehand with a brush and plant-based dyes. In Shipibo-Konibo belief the patterns are tied to song and to visions of the Amazon, so the paintings work as a kind of written music. One work also appears as a flag flying above the space.

The show, curated by Issela Ccoyllo and Matteo Norzi, brings an Amazonian way of seeing into the heart of the contemporary art circuit.

shows.title: Sea of Love / Dagat ng Pag-ibig
shows.description:
Jon Cuyson's pavilion is a tribute to Filipino seafarers, the workers who keep global shipping moving and are rarely seen. In the Arsenale he builds a ship-like interior of weathered steel panels, salt-crusted and blue-stained, with heavy anchor chain spilling across the floor and small monitors set into the walls.

The screens play black-and-white film: men hauling sacks onto a boat, a diver wrapped in mussels and coral, hands at work, a woman looking out from the trees, and a sailor on a phone far from home. Painting, sculpture, sound and moving image are used together so that the room feels like a hold, a deck and a memory of home at once.

Curated by Mara Gladstone, it is the Philippines' sixth appearance since 2015 and frames love as the thing that keeps migrant workers going.

shows.title: Liquid Tongues
shows.description:
Bogna Burska and Daniel Kotowski present a large-scale audio-video installation shot underwater. A choir of hearing and Deaf performers in red and white move through lakes and a swimming pool, shaping the communication codes of whales and other sea animals into sign and gesture.

The film is projected on a wide screen in a darkened hall with a low platform for visitors to lie on, so viewers take in the images, mirrored crowds of swimmers, close-ups of bare feet and hands pressed against the water's surface, while hearing sound built from whale song. The piece links Deaf culture, which has long been marginalised, with non-human ways of speaking.

It asks what counts as language and who is listened to, and was chosen from 95 proposals in Poland's open competition for the pavilion.

shows.title: RedSkyFalls
shows.description:
Alexandre Estrela's RedSkyFalls is an artificial ecosystem in the Fondaco Marcello that reacts to seismic activity around the world. A very large screen shows a mountain lake landscape, with smaller screens, speakers and light panels scattered around it, all driven by earthquake data.

The artist has spoken of the unsettling gap between a seismic event and the way it is represented. Copies of the project, called replicas, were hosted at the same time in San Francisco, Los Angeles, Lima, Mexico City and Lisbon, so the work lives across several places at once.

Ana Baliza and Ricardo Nicolau curate the pavilion.

venue.name: Portugal Pavilion
venue.address: Fondaco Marcello, Calle del traghetto o Ca’ Garzoni, San Marco 3415

shows.title: Untitled (A gathering of remarkable people)
shows.artist: Rirkrit Tiravanija, Sophia Al Maria, Tarek Atoui, Alia Farid, Fadi Kattan
shows.description:
Rirkrit Tiravanija has put an open, tent-like pavilion in the Giardini, with a deep red roof and a floor patterned in a geometric Arab design. It is meant as a place to gather, in the spirit of Gulf and wider Arab traditions of hospitality, rather than a space of objects to look at.

Four collaborators fill it with activity. Tarek Atoui organises live music performances inspired by the classical Arab orchestra and its suites, and Sophia Al-Maria contributes a film shown on a screen under the roof. Alia Farid's large pale vessel, Jerrican, modelled on Gulf water containers, stands in the middle, and the chef Fadi Kattan serves reinterpretations of harees, a wheat and meat dish eaten across the region.

Curated by Tom Eccles and Ruba Katrib, the project treats food, sound and conversation as the work itself.

shows.title: Black Seas – Scores for the Sonic Eye
shows.description:
Anca Benera and Arnold Estefán treat the Black Sea as a living archive and a place of tension, and the show runs across two sites. In the Giardini pavilion, a dark blue room holds hanging buoy-like sculptures, a red marker covered in sea growth, and large screens showing waves, fishing nets, and a figure sitting by the water.

At a second space in Cannaregio, a white room shows a silvery tower sculpture made from layered marine and scientific forms beside wall drawings, while a bank of screens plays underwater footage and satellite-style imagery. A glass case holds samples under blue light.

The pair combine science, sound and sculpture to read the sea through its sonic traces, asking what can be heard in a body of water shaped by war, trade and ecological change. The project was curated by Corina Oprea and Diana Marincu.

shows.title: Sea of Sound
shows.description:
Mark Francis, a Northern Irish painter, shows large new abstract paintings in a former timber and coal warehouse between the Arsenale and the Giardini. Their blurred vertical bands of colour take cues from sound: low frequencies, ambient noise and the range of vibrations people live in without hearing.

The entry room screens a film, Listening Field, and a second room holds the canvases, many of them never shown before. The pavilion's title, Sea of Sound, refers to the vastness of the frequencies that surround us.

Luca Tommasi curates for San Marino, and a related show is planned in San Marino itself from December.

venue.name: San Marino Pavilion
venue.address: Tana Art Space, Fondamenta de la Tana, Castello 2111

shows.title: May your tears never dry, you who weep over stones
shows.description:
Dana Awartani covers the floor of the Saudi pavilion in the Arsenale with a huge mosaic made of about 29,000 handmade clay bricks. Four clays from different parts of Saudi Arabia give the bricks their ochre, brown, cream and dark tones, and the patterns echo geometric floors from mosque and palace traditions across the Islamic world.

The floor is broken and incomplete, as if the visitor were looking at an excavated site, and the piece is a lament for architecture and cultural heritage lost to war and neglect. Dozens of artisans in Saudi Arabia worked with the artist to cut and lay the pieces.

Curated by Antonia Carver, it carries Awartani's own family story of displacement from Palestine, and it is the fifth appearance of Saudi Arabia at the main exhibition.

shows.title: « WURUS* »
shows.description:
Caroline Gueye, an artist who also holds degrees in astrophysics and atomic physics, builds her Senegal installation around gold. Wall sculptures in brass and bronze-toned polymer echo the architecture of the Palazzo Navagero, and a light piece glows in an adjoining room.

Wurus, meaning what the earth offers us, asks how value becomes visible rather than simply putting gold on display. The lattice forms read like cells, nets or star maps, and the gold shifts as the light changes.

Massamba Mbaye curates. Senegal is also present in a separate Biennale project with Seni Camara and Issa Samb.

venue.name: Senegal Pavilion
venue.address: Palazzo Navagero Gallery, Riva degli Schiavoni, Castello 4145

shows.title: Through Golgotha to Resurrection
shows.description:
Predrag Djaković fills the walls of Serbia's Giardini pavilion with an archive he has been assembling for years, roughly forty large panels made of old photographs, maps, personal papers and official documents laid edge to edge. Together they try to build a visual history of the twentieth century out of everyday fragments.

Suitcases recur through the show as a sign of the forced journeys that marked the period, and a video features the artist playing a piano piece of his own. The title uses Golgotha for the collapse of a system of values and resurrection as an open question.

The curator is Tomáš Koudela. The choice of artist was disputed at home, with a petition signed by hundreds of Serbian cultural workers, so the pavilion arrived in Venice with a political backstory.

shows.title: Seychelles - Existence on an island
shows.description:
Egbert Marday, a former biology teacher who trained in fine arts in Canada, makes Seychelles' first appearance at the Biennale with a single work, Spiritual Journey from 2015. A figure of a seated musician sits in a small niche room, a quiet image of island life and its music.

The pavilion is organised with the European Cultural Centre at Palazzo Mora, under the title Existence on an Island, and is curated by Nina Comini.

It was added to the official list after the first announcement of national participations.

venue.name: Seychelles Pavilion
venue.address: European Cultural Centre, Strada Nova, Cannaregio 3659

shows.title: Worlds of Today
shows.artist: Hawa-Jane Bangura, Ayesha Feisal, Hickmatu Bintu Leigh, Abu Bakarr Mansaray, Seyni Awa Camara, Abdoul Ganiou Dermani, Eloi Lokossou, Móyòsóré Martins, Eros Bonamini, Piergiorgio Colombara, Jacopo Di Cera Alberto Salvetti, Fernando Garbellotto, Gianfranco Gentile, Armando Amaya Romero, Margherita Levo Rosenberg
shows.description:
Sierra Leone makes its Biennale debut with Worlds of Today, a group show in the Guggenheim art high school in Dorsoduro. It brings Sierra Leonean artists together with artists from West Africa and Italy, so that local and international practices share a room.

Named participants include Hawa-Jane Bangura, Ayesha Feisal, Hickmatu Bintu Leigh, Abu Bakarr Mansaray and Seyni Awa Camara, alongside several Italian and other artists. Sandro Orlandi Stagl and Willy Montini curate, and the commissioner is H. E. Fatima Maada Bio.

It is one of four African countries taking part for the first time this year.

venue.name: Sierra Leone Pavilion
venue.address: Liceo Artistico Statale Michelangelo Guggenheim, Dorsoduro 2613

shows.title: A Pause
shows.description:
Amanda Heng's pavilion is built around rest. On the Arsenale's upper floor, a curved wooden enclosure and a set of broad wooden steps invite visitors to sit, lean or lie down, while a two-channel video plays on the curved wall. The film was shot in both Venice and Singapore and shows ordinary acts of pausing: sitting, stretching, resting a body.

Leaning against the walls are framed photographs and works that continue the theme, and tall arched windows look out over the lagoon light. Heng, a pioneer of performance art in Singapore, has long made work about everyday gestures, the body and women's labour, and here she asks visitors to slow down in the middle of a very busy Biennale.

It is Singapore's twelfth participation in the main exhibition, curated by Selene Yap of the Singapore Art Museum.

shows.title: Soundtrack for an Invisible House
shows.artist: Nonument Group (Neja Tomšič, Martin Bricelj Baraga, Nika Grabar, Miloš Kosec)
shows.description:
Nonument Group have turned Slovenia's Arsenale space into a dark, ruin-like landscape of broken concrete blocks, bricks and dust, assembled from waste left by earlier Biennale pavilions. A bare platform sits in the middle, with a sound sculpture over it that works as both a shelter and an amplifier.

The piece is about a wooden mosque built by Austro-Hungarian soldiers in 1917 at Log pod Mangartom, in the Slovenian Alps, which no longer exists as a building. The group went back to the meadow where it stood, recorded the silence and surrounding sounds there, and overlaid an old photograph of the mosque onto a relief map of the mountains. Those recordings are played back in Venice.

The four artists call this kind of project a nonument, a memorial that works through absence and listening. The pavilion was curated by Nataša Petrešin-Bachelez.

shows.title: Saddexleey
shows.artist: Ayan Farah, Asmaa Jama, Warsan Shire
shows.description:
Somalia's first national pavilion takes its name from a Somali poetic form built in threes, and it is laid out the same way across the three floors of Palazzo Caboto. Warsan Shire's poetry greets visitors, Asmaa Jama's film and installation follow, and Ayan Farah's textile works close the route.

Jama builds an audiovisual space where voices recombine into shifting landscapes of the self, while Farah's large panels are dyed with soil and layered like sediment, so that cloth reads as stratified time. Scent and sound run through the rooms alongside the images.

The pavilion has also drawn public criticism from Somali artists and cultural groups about how it was organised, which is part of the story of this debut.

shows.title: Los restos
shows.description:
Oriol Vilanova covers the walls of the Spanish Pavilion with thousands of vintage postcards, hung edge to edge so the rooms read as one continuous mural. The cards come from more than twenty years of buying at flea markets and second-hand shops. They are sorted into groups by subject: flowers, ships, desert dunes, strange rocks, rows of souvenirs. Strips of a single colour run through the wall like seams.

Most of the cards were once written on, sent and then thrown out. Pulled away from the places they once pictured, they stop working as views of monuments and become small leftovers of ordinary lives. A bilingual atlas of the collection, published by Walther Konig, accompanies the show.

Curated by Carles Guerra, the project turns the pavilion into a stand-in museum that has no hierarchy and no story to finish, asking what is left when memory is passed through cheap, everyday objects.

shows.title: The Unfinished Business of Living Together
shows.artist: Miriam Laura Leonardi, Lithic Alliance, Yul Tomatala, Nina Wakeford
shows.description:
The Swiss Pavilion starts from two live television debates, Telearena in 1978 and the French-language Agora in 1984, in which gay people spoke publicly in Switzerland for the first time and then faced the consequences at work and at home. The team treats those broadcasts as an archive that can still be used, replaying and restaging them rather than just remembering them.

The show is built around a spatialised video work that blends archival television footage with newly shot scenes, voices and sets. Rooms inside Bruno Giacometti's pavilion hold screens, a television set in the wall, props, costumes and a shark-shaped sculpture, so the debate format becomes a physical environment you walk through.

Behind it is a larger question about what it means to share a country: how the state, the media and the family define who counts, and how that coexistence stays unresolved. Six people share authorship, each asking where memory lives and which histories must be invented.

shows.title: The Tower Tomb of Palmyra
shows.description:
Sara Shamma, the first Syrian artist to hold a solo presentation at the Biennale, builds a full-scale tower tomb in a courtyard of the Iuav campus. Inside, monumental figurative paintings inspired by the funerary reliefs of Palmyra line a circular chamber, with sound and the scent of desert landscape.

The real tower tombs of Palmyra were destroyed in the war and many reliefs were looted, so the installation re-creates a lost form of coexistence rather than only mourning it. Shamma first drew Palmyrene reliefs as a student in Damascus, and her heavily worked, gesture-filled figures come from that long interest in portraiture and the psychology of suffering.

The pictures shown here are her paintings of the last decade, because the pavilion's own paintings are not posted individually.

shows.title: Minor Frequencies: The Inner Life Of A Nation
shows.artist: Amani Abeid, Valerie Asiimwe Amani, Turakella Editha Gyindo, Lazaro Samuel, Silvia Canton, Maria Elisabetta Novello
shows.description:
Minor Frequencies asks visitors to listen to the background noise of a nation rather than its slogans. Tanzanian artists share the rooms with a chorus of invited artists from elsewhere, and the work is organised around four lines of inquiry: body, gesture, archive and mind.

It is a very large roster, 35 artists, hosted by the Gervasuti Foundation in Cannaregio, and curated by Lorna Benedict Mashiba and Martina Cavallarin.

Tanzanian participants include Amani Abeid, Valerie Asiimwe Amani, Turakella Editha Gyindo and Lazaro Samuel.

venue.name: Tanzania Pavilion
venue.address: Gervasuti Foundation at Supernova, Fondamenta della Sensa, Cannaregio 3218/A

shows.title: Across Words
shows.artist: Verónica Pereira Maia, Etson Caminha, Juventino Madeira
shows.description:
Across Words puts language at the centre of Timor-Leste's identity, a young country where many tongues live side by side. The heart of the pavilion is Tais Don, a huge woven textile begun in 1994 by Verónica Pereira Maia, stitched with the names of people lost during the Indonesian occupation and now hung from the ceiling of the Arsenale.

Around it are video works and sound by Etson Caminha and Juventino Madeira, shown on stacks of screens, including a work by the youngest artist in the pavilion that overlays voices and faces in red and blue. Together they treat speech, naming and memory as the way a nation holds itself together.

The pavilion, curated by Loredana Pazzini Paracciani, is the country's second at the Biennale and is accompanied by an anthology on Timor-Leste's contemporary art.

shows.title: Kampala
shows.artist: Joseph Ntensibe, Lilian Mary Nabulime, Ronex Ahimbisibwe, Lakwena Maciver, Sheila Nakitende, Stacey Gillian Abe, Aloka Mark Trevor
shows.description:
Uganda returns to Venice with a large group show titled Kampala, set in Palazzo Navagero on the Riva degli Schiavoni. Seven artists, among them Stacey Gillian Abe, Joseph Ntensibe, Lilian Mary Nabulime, Ronex Ahimbisibwe, Lakwena Maciver, Sheila Nakitende and Aloka Trevor, take the city as a lens on material culture, spirituality and social memory.

The show is curated by Taga Francis Nuwagaba under commissioner Acaye Kerunen, who also led the country's first pavilion in 2022.

Abe's Garden of Blue Whispers has drawn the most press attention so far.

venue.name: Uganda Pavilion
venue.address: Palazzo Navagero Gallery, Riva degli Schiavoni, Castello 4147

shows.title: Security Guarantees
shows.description:
Ukraine's pavilion is built around a single rescued sculpture, Zhanna Kadyrova's Origami Deer. Made in 2019 for a park in Pokrovsk, it was pulled out of the frontline zone during the 2024 evacuation and carried across Europe before arriving in Venice, where it is shown hoisted in public space outside the Giardini.

The title points to the assurances Ukraine was given in 1994 when it handed over its nuclear weapons. Inside the Arsenale, video documentation and archive material trace the deer's journey from town to town, so the object becomes evidence as much as sculpture.

Kadyrova is known for turning rubble and everyday building materials into monuments; the pictures added here of her Palianytsia stones belong to that practice.

shows.title: Washwasha
shows.artist: Mays Albaik, Jawad Al Malhi, Farah Al Qasimi, Alaa Edris, Lamya Gargash, Taus Makhacheva
shows.description:
Washwasha is an Arabic word for whispering, and the UAE pavilion treats the whisper as a way of passing on memory, rumour and belonging when speech is not public. Six artists contribute works that use sound, voice and the spaces between people.

Visitors move through a dim, brick-walled room of listening stations where headphones play oral recollections beside small screens, then reach a black space where carved wooden faces hang in the dark and a wall of red curtain scattered with tiny objects, cartoon figures and a screen. A white circular chamber pierced with holes ends the route.

The project, curated by Bana Kattan, follows migration and the languages that travel with it in the Gulf, and picks up the Biennale's minor-keys theme by working at low volume.

shows.title: Call Me the Breeze
shows.description:
Alma Allen fills the neoclassical US Pavilion with sculptures that look as if they had been worn into shape by wind and water. Pieces in walnut burl, volcanic cantera, Colorado Yule marble and cast bronze sit in bright white rooms: a hollow marble ring, tall twisting columns of banded stone, wall-hung slabs of bronze and wood, and gilded forms that seem to pour like liquid. In the forecourt, new black bronzes, including a headless sheep, meet visitors before they go inside.

Allen, a self-taught sculptor born in Utah who works from Tepoztlan in Mexico, models small clay forms by hand and then enlarges them with a robotic carver, finishing every surface by hand. The results read as seed pods, roots, fossils or torsos, and refuse to settle into any one category.

The show is built around the idea of elevation, both as shape and as a hopeful, forward-looking mood, and it arrives as the United States approaches its 250th anniversary. It is also among the most talked-about pavilions of the year because of how the choice of Allen was made and received.

shows.title: Antifragile
shows.description:
Margaret Whyte fills Uruguay's pavilion with a single installation made from fabric, discarded machinery and heaps of rubble. Quilted, patched textile forms rise out of the debris like bodies half buried or half emerging, and the room is lit so that each pile reads as its own small landscape.

The title borrows the idea that some systems get stronger from disorder rather than being broken by it. Whyte, who has worked with sewing, domestic labour and recycled material for decades, makes ruin and repair look like the same gesture.

The work suits a biennale themed around minor keys: it is quiet, tactile and humble in its materials, and it asks visitors to look closely at what is normally swept away.

shows.title: The Aural Sea
shows.artist: Jahongir Bobokulov, Zi Kakhramonova, Aygul Sarsen, Zulfiya Spowart, Xin Liu, A.A.Murakami, Nguyen Phuong Linh
shows.description:
The Aural Sea takes the vanished Aral Sea as its starting point: a body of water that left salt, sand and stories behind. Seven artists respond with sculpture, painting, installation and sound, all in a hall of the Arsenale laid with sand and pale glass.

Works on view include red metallic sheets lying like wrecked sails, vitrines glowing with sea-coloured light, a carved wall that looks like frozen waves, a glowing orange disc and a group of small figurative paintings. Water here is something to hear and to remember as much as to see.

The pavilion links Central Asia's ecological history to ideas of listening and memory, and brings together artists living in Uzbekistan and abroad.

shows.title: Viet Nam: Art in the Global Flow
shows.artist: Nguyen Thanh Chuong, Doan Thi Thu Huong, Bui Huu Hung, Le Hoang Nguyen, Trinh Tuan, Cong Kim Hoa, Dinh Van Quan, Dinh Thi Tham Poong, Oanh Phi Phi, Nguyen Truong Linh, Trieu Khac Tien, Le Nguyen Chinh, Le Huu Hieu
shows.description:
Viet Nam's first national pavilion, in the Gothic Ca' Faccanon, gathers ten artists around lacquer, a traditional craft the show treats as a living contemporary language. Le Huu Hieu's installation Tam is the headline work.

The title Art in the Global Flow frames the presentation as a way of putting Vietnamese practice into conversation with international art. The artists include Bui Huu Hung, Doan Thi Thu Huong and Le Nguyen Chinh.

Commissioner is Ma The Anh and curator Do Tuong Linh, for the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism.

venue.name: Viet nam Pavilion
venue.address: Ca’ Faccanon, Calle delle Acque, San Marco 5016

shows.title: Second Nature | Manyonga
shows.artist: Gideon Gomo, Eva Raath, Felix Shumba, Franklyn Dzingai, Pardon Mapondera
shows.description:
Second Nature | Manyonga brings five Zimbabwean artists together in Santa Maria della Pietà under curator Fadzai Veronica Muchemwa. Gideon Gomo makes sculptural assemblages of stone, metal and found objects, Franklyn Dzingai prints with a reductive cardboard method, Pardon Mapondera builds textile compositions from recycled plastic, Eva Raath prints large textiles on identity and transformation, and Felix Shumba works across drawing, video and installation.

The pavilion is commissioned by Raphael Chikukwa of the National Gallery of Zimbabwe.

shows.description:
Le parole e le cose marks fifteen years of CASADOROFUNGHER, a Venice communications studio that works with artists and cultural projects. More than thirty works from the collection assembled by its founders, Elena Casadoro Kopp and Francesca Fungher, are shown, by ten artists including Giulio Alvigini, Matteo Attruia, H-E-C-K, Manuel Gualandi, Giovanni Morbin, Penzo+Fiore, Paolo Pretolani, Eleonora Rinaldi, Pierluigi Slis and Lucia Veronesi.

The title borrows from Michel Foucault's 1966 book on language and representation. Two rooms follow two ideas: the first, named for a preparatory sketch for Tintoretto's Paradiso that hangs there, gathers works built from words and language; the second looks at relationships and the chance and contingency of meeting people, through a wider selection of paintings, drawings, collage and photography.

Curated by Luca Berta, Daniele Capra and Francesca Giubilei, the show reads as a portrait of a studio through the art it has lived with, set in the rooms of the Palazzo Contarini del Bovolo.
